speechtext:

subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  REFERENCE TO ANSWER BY MIN- ISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE ON MAY 18
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. On Friday of last week in response to a question I put to the Minister of Trade and Commerce on three occasions regarding Trans-Canada's option to purchase pipe in the United States the minister stated, as recorded on page 4068 of Hansard for May 18, that the option had been translated into a firm contract and that he would table a copy of that contract either Friday or Monday. Yesterday, his parliamentary assistant tabled a document which had been labelled as sessional paper No. 174-S, which I presume is the contract referred to by the minister on Friday.
My point of privilege, Mr. Speaker, is that since the minister said this was a firm contract there must be something missing from this voluminous sessional paper, for in at least three places in this sessional paper it says clearly that Trans-Canada's option to purchase the pipe is still contingent upon Tennessee letting Trans-Canada know that it has obtained all the necessary licences and permits to import gas into the United States. Therefore, I should like to know from the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether there are any other documents or any portions of this agreement which he has not tabled, in view of his statement last Friday that what he would table would be a firm contract.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  REFERENCE TO ANSWER BY MIN- ISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE ON MAY 18
speechtext:
My reference to a firm contract-a contract involving payments from a non-existent company cannot be a firm contract. If the hon. member will look

at the correct document he will see that as soon as assurance can be given that the necessary legislation has been obtained on or before June 7 of this year, an indication of that fact will make the document a firm contract. Naturally, you just cannot get a firm contract until the government can do its part. By whom would the firm contract be implemented?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  REFERENCE TO ANSWER BY MIN- ISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE ON MAY 18
speechtext:
Is the minister aware that the agreement itself which is at the beginning of this document tabled yesterday says that, in addition to the passing of the bill now before parliament, the conditions set out in exhibit A to exhibits I and II of this document must be met? Is he aware of the fact that in at least two covering letters it is stated by Tennessee, Hudson Bay and Canadian Gulf that clause 2 of the stock option agreement is still in force, and that that clause 2 of the stock option agreement which appears twice in this document says that, and I quote from clause 2:
Tennessee shall assign such purchase orders to Trans-Canada within sixty (60) days after Tennessee has notified Trans-Canada that there have been obtained all certificates, licences and permits which, in the judgment of Tennessee, are necessary and sufficient to authorize Midwestern Gas Transmission Company, a Delaware corporation affiliated with Tennessee, to construct and operate a natural gas transmission pipe line system extending from the international boundary near Emerson, Manitoba, to connect in the state of Tennessee with the pipe line system of Tennessee and to take gas from Trans-Canada at Emerson, Manitoba.
Is the minister not aware that his whole case, which is based on getting this pipe, falls to the ground, since this is not a firm contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  REFERENCE TO ANSWER BY MIN- ISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE ON MAY 18
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am advised that the contract can be firm the day after the legislation is passed.

subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  REFERENCE TO ANSWER BY MIN- ISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE ON MAY 18

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  REFERENCE TO ANSWER BY MIN- ISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE ON MAY 18

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  REFERENCE TO ANSWER BY MIN- ISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE ON MAY 18

Mr. Speaker, the minister's words on Friday were these:
In the meantime, the option has been translated into a firm contract, and the contract has attached to it certain mill orders and other documents which are now being examined, and I hope to be able to table the contract either today or Monday.
I am prepared to submit this document to any impartial examiner and I am sure he will agree with me it is not a firm contract but is a contract that is still conditional

upon Tennessee being satisfied that it has what it regards as the appropriate permits and licences.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, May 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) for the second reading of Bill No. 298, to establish the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONSTITUTION OF CROWN COMPANY TO CONSTRUCT PIPE LINE, MAKE SHORT-TERM LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the 20 minutes now allowed to us under the shadow of the axe I shall not be able to cover many of the subjects that I would have liked to discuss. I do wish to refer briefly once again to this extraordinary procedure in regard to which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has not had a word to say. We have had here the unprecedented use, and I should say "abuse", of closure, and I would like to bring the memories of some hon. members back to the objections that were raised on two earlier occasions to a procedure which followed an extended debate. On August 29, 1917, as reported at page 5121 of Hansard for that day, Sir Wilfrid Laurier had this to say, and I suggest that the words perhaps have an almost reminiscent sound:
The Minister of Finance has said that the debate upon this bill has lasted two weeks. I do not know that it should have lasted any shorter time than that. The question is one of the most important that we have ever had before us; it is full of complications; it is full of figures.
On this occasion, Mr. Speaker, the debate on the bill lasted two days before closure was moved, not two weeks, and when we had a motion before us for the introduction of this bill closure was moved before there had been any debate at all and before the minister introducing the measure had even heard a word of what the opposition had to say on this bill. Precedents have a habit of becoming established customs. This is a dangerous precedent, indeed. In the past, offensive though it may have been to many of the hon. members, closure followed extended debate and was employed at least with some colour of justification. Here closure is simply a bald threat to the opposition that they are not going
4170	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation to be permitted to place their case before parliament and above all before the people of Canada so that the opinion of the people of Canada can express itself.
These are dangerous precedents. This puts parliament in chains and, therefore, if carried a stage farther, would make parliament ineffective as a place for the conduct of the business of the people of Canada. What have we before us now? Something that the government knew about for a long time. When we heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) yesterday one would have thought that this was a perfectly obvious course which everyone would follow naturally. Why, the government itself did not know two weeks ago what it was going to do. The backbenchers opposite did not know until last week what the government had decided to do. For four months and more we have been waiting for word of what would be done, and it was only after long and painful discussion within the cabinet itself that a decision was reached, and now we are told that everybody should follow this course simply because it comes from this omniscient government. They say it is right and therefore it must be. That is as far as the argument goes. There was not one word from the Minister of Finance, and certainly not a word from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), as to why this mongrel bill has been placed before us in this manner.
We have two distinct measures incorporated in one bill, the one that they originally intended to present and the one that now really is the nub of the discussion before us. The bill that was announced on January 10 was an act to establish the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation, and that was to build the difficult stretch through northern Ontario. Now, we have something entirely different. Now we have the construction of the easiest part of all from the Alberta boundary to the vicinity of Winnipeg. This separate part is to be found on page 6 of Bill 298 as printed and handed out. It is headed "Part II. Western Section." Western section of what? Western section of the northern Ontario pipe line, to be built by the crown corporation. Well, it is just as fantastic as that because the earlier part of the bill deals entirely with the construction of the northern Ontario bridge with money provided by the government to the crown corporation. That is what it is, an outrageous transaction for which Canadian money is used to hand over the control of one of our greatest resources to a company that is 83 per cent owned by United States investors. Then, so that this transaction will look slightly palatable, an arrangement is made for the approximately 575 miles to be


financed by the government by granting to the crown corporation $80 million which may be advanced by the crown corporation to the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines for the construction of this western section.
This mongrel bill has not been explained. There has been no attempt to tell us why we have not a single bill before us to incorporate the whole of this, or why we are not dealing with a single bill under which the government would frankly and honestly place before us its purpose today, and that is to advance the money to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines for the construction of that western section, because, Mr. Speaker, the northern Ontario bridge cannot be built as long as the transaction set out in part II stands. As long as that money is outstanding, the northern Ontario bridge cannot be built because there will not be the money in the treasury of the crown corporation to construct any substantial part of it.
On the face of it this bill is a fraud. Let the government honestly bring in a bill and, bad though the proposition may be, put that proposition frankly before us and ask for permission to advance money directly to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines for that western section and not pretend that that has anything whatever to do with the construction by a crown corporation, which is an agency of the government, of what has been described by the minister as the difficult northern Ontario bridge.
There is more than that in it, Mr. Speaker. There is also a joker clause in part II. In section 7, subsection (1), we find this at the very beginning:
Pursuant to an agreement in that behalf made, with the approval of the governor in council, before or after the coming into force of this act . . .
Now, Mr. Speaker, that means that any measure coming in after this act would be covered by this act. We do not know whether the agreement tabled is the agreement that is binding upon the government. Any new agreement under this act brought in afterwards to amend that earlier act would be effective under the terms of this act. This is bad in every respect. It lacks frankness; it lacks candor and it provides a joker clause which makes it possible for this government once more to vary the transaction without parliament knowing what it is doing.
Then, in so far as the sessional paper that was tabled yesterday is concerned, to which reference has been made, there again is lack of frankness. That sessional paper makes it perfectly clear that the options on the pipe are not transferred by Tennessee Gas to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines until there is approval of the importation of gas into the

United States by the agency of the government of the United States, namely, the federal power commission in Washington.

Actually, there is one provision in this that will call for a lot of explanation and one reason why this should go before the committee. There is a great deal of doubt as to whether Tennessee Gas would give up the ownership of that pipe line at any time under this agreement which has been tabled until the federal power commission has actually given the permission that is sought. That is the reason we have asked that this whole matter go before a committee. On May 17 we moved that this be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. A sub-amendment was moved to the effect that these words be added:
So that consideration might be given to the advisability of recommending the constructing and operating of a trans-Canada natural gas pipe line under public ownership.
Mr. Speaker, I would point out that our amendment referring this whole matter to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines embraces the subject matter of this sub-amendment, and on the other hand the sub-amendment would have the effect of limiting what could go before that committee. As this would read, it would be that this would be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines so that consideration might be given to the advisability of recommending the constructing and operating of a trans-Canada natural gas pipe line under public ownership. We do not intend to support a proposal that would strangle the committee which we have asked to have set up. The committee we have asked to have this referred to would have full power to inquire into the subject matter but it would also have power to inquire into some of the statements made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe).

Second, insist upon the reorganization of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines as an all-Canadian company which can proceed immediately and under Canadian control. Mr. Speaker, those words are clear; they are not open to mistake. We have asked that this procedure be followed and we ask that it be followed now. On the pipe line, the government now proposes not only to turn over a vital natural resource to foreign control, permanently, but is actually prepared to finance this ill-conceived project with public money, the benefit to go mainly to the United States, and the profits to go to private United States interests.
It is a most strange kind of "declaration of independence" to sell out part of our national heritage to private foreign interests and force the Canadian taxpayer to finance the sell-out.
The Trans-Canada Pipe Lines deal is a bad dream of Mr. Howe's.
To liken it to the seaway project is a hideous nightmare.
That appeared in the Calgary Herald on May 10; a responsible publication right in the very heart of the area from which this gas would be coming.

With respect to the statement made by the hon. gentleman that there is a joker in the bill because it refers to contracts which have been made or which may be made, I would refer him to the first clause of the act which was passed by the legislature of Ontario and which is cited in the letter addressed by Mr. Porter to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). This letter was read into the record of this house on May 17. The second to the last paragraph of the letter reads:
In any matter of such complexity and magnitude, we recognize that it may become necessary to consider changes in arrangements from time to time. At the last session of the legislature an act was passed, by the unanimous recorded vote of the house, giving authority to enter into such arrangements. The act allows for certain flexibility so as to meet changing situations as they may arise. Section 1 of the act is as follows:
"1. For the purpose of implementing the arrangements made or to be made between the government of Canada and the government of Ontario to facilitate the construction of a connecting link through northern Ontario of a pipe line to transport natural gas from Alberta into central Ontario, the treasurer of Ontario is hereby authorized to loan from time to time-''
Why is this bill before the house? We submit that it is the first proper and necessary step to implement what has been Canadian policy for the last half century, a policy which was sanctioned by legislation introduced and recommended to this parliament in 1907, that is to say to preserve for Canadians energy and power produced in Canada to the full extent required by actual or future probable requirements of Canadians. That policy has been followed and has been approved-I think it is still approved-by every hon. member of this house and by the public generally.
A fact that cannot be denied is that there are tremendous amounts of gas being produced in Alberta beyond the requirements of that province, gas which those who produce it wish to dispose of and which people in other parts of Canada can use and wish to use, and which will in being properly used
4174	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation within Canada continue to promote and stimulate this era of extraordinary development that has been going on in this country for the last several years.
That requires the construction of the pipe line from Alberta to central Canada. That is the longest pipe line ever undertaken for the transmission of gas. It is a considerable undertaking. It is an undertaking which we and many others, including the prime minister of Manitoba, the government of Ontario and the prime minister of Alberta, felt should be started at the earliest possible moment. This bill is before the house because, after carefully considering all possibilities, we came to the conclusion that this was the only practicable way to get the construction of this line started this summer and completed from the Alberta boundary to Winnipeg before the end of this construction season.
I know that our socialist friends pretend that that is not the way to do it, that it should be done as a public enterprise owned and administered by a public authority in Canada. That has been carefully considered, and the reasons for the objections-they are not insuperable objections, but the reasons for objecting to that-as the most desirable course to be followed, are grave reasons, reasons that have impressed the government of Ontario, which gave them consideration too, as they have impressed us. The prime minister of Ontario has said-and his words have been read into the record here-that, if private industry can do the job, it is in the interests of Ontario and in the interests of all Canada that private enterprise do the job, but that, if it fails, if it cannot be done otherwise, it is a matter of such importance that the serious difficulties involved in public ownership would have to be faced and have to be overcome.
That line should be built and it will be built, and the future generations of Canadians will be glad that it will have been built. It is an important factor in maintaining the impetus of the Canadian economy that has been so gratifying during these last years. There have been suggestions that there were many other things that should be done. All those other things may be very desirable things, but they cannot all be done at once. I am sure all members of the house were impressed yesterday by the statement made by the Minister of Finance on the serious consideration his department gave-and it is not an attractive proposal to any Minister of Finance to make loans of public funds, even for a short term and even at the ordinary commercial rates of interest-but after examining the whole situation he came to the conclusion- and he stated that conclusion to the house


yesterday-that it was a good thing for the economy of Canada generally and, incidentally, that it would be a very good thing for the public treasury because of the participation of the public treasury in the profits that are made out of any of the industries that are being established and exploited in the Canadian economy.
The hon. gentleman caused some amusement when he said that that would provide money with which all these other things could be done. He was then asked if that was a promise, that as soon as this was completed all those other things would be done. Well, that is something which no one could undertake, because careful consideration has to be given to all these enterprises that are all good and that all contribute to the welfare of the Canadian nation but that cannot all be accomplished at the same time.
Why did we come to the conclusion that Trans-Canada was the instrument that could and should be used to bring about the start of this line this season? It is because it appeared to us that it was the only practicable way in which work could be started this season and proceeded with in a manner that would make for completion of the leg from the Alberta boundary to Winnipeg before the close of this season. I think that that is a fact that cannot be disputed.
Why was it the only agency? It was the only agency that had the permits; the only agency that had the plans; the only agency that had the organization; the only agency that had the pipe, under these arrangements, which are covered by the agreements that have now been tabled in the house.

Now, sir, the reason we are particularly interested in the observations I have just quoted is that, as everyone knows, any pipe line company has to take care of three items. First of all the interest upon its debt, which in this case would be the 5 per cent to the government; second, its wages and other operating costs; third, the price of its gas. In that connection it is under the necessity in delivering this gas to take into account not only the distance from the place where the gas originates to the market but the character of the market itself. It is perfectly clear that the cost of the operation of a pipe line does not decrease very much regardless of the quantity of gas which is put through it during the course of a year. That being so, if it will put through, let us say, 1,000 million cubic feet per year at full operation but if the markets which it serves will only take 800 million cubic feet, then because under this 80 per cent load factor the smaller amount of gas is going through, a higher rate must be charged per unit in order to meet the cost of operation of the pipe line. The real significance so far as Winnipeg, Toronto or any other community that can be reached by the pipe line is concerned is the necessity for quick action. The fact that the government adopted a rather unusual course in regard to this agreement and did not, as my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre has pointed out, include it as a schedule to the bill, indicates that they wanted to leave some gate open for future negotiations with the Trans-Canada company, and certainly our past experiences with this company would indicate that almost anything might happen.
The other day I noticed that my friend, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier), and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) were digging into their scriptural inheritance of interesting texts. It stirred up some of the admittedly very faint scriptural memories of my own, but I thought of something else. I was reminded, Mr. Speaker, of the daughter of the horse leech forever shouting "more", and it occurred to me that the enterprising lady had moved to Texas or perhaps to Ottawa to carry on her operations. Or


we might even have another scriptural reference, Mr. Speaker. We on this side of the house at least are left in the frame of mind of the queen of Sheba when she was confronted with all the glories of Solomon and said, "Behold, not half has been told me".
I suspect, Mr. Speaker, that not half has been told us yet. I suspect that as time goes on and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) continues his entertaining dance of the seven veils and reveals a little bit more with every turn we may find out some other things. In addition to finding out as we did today that there are no firm contracts for pipe, although the minister told us quite definitely there were some, we may also find that there are no firm agreements with respect to the construction of other parts of this line.
There has been what is to my mind a very interesting and rather suspicious silence on the part of the minister and other members of the government with regard to the construction of that part of the line that lies between Winnipeg and the Ontario boundary and that part of the line which lies between Kapus-kasing and the eastern markets for Canadian gas. There may be some agreement. None has been tabled in the house and under the terms of this legislation it would make very little difference if one were tabled in the house because it might last for a week, it might last for a month, it might last for a year, depending, I presume, on the exigencies of this poverty stricken group of American financiers.
I see nothing in the agreement that we have before us which may not be superseded and nothing in the bill which tells me quite plainly, if and when Trans-Canada by some mysterious means gets the pipe before the F.P.C. gives them a ruling and constructs the western part of the line to Winnipeg, I see nothing in the statements of the minister or of the three or four of his colleagues who have spoken, nothing that indicates to me that this government has a firm undertaking from Trans-Canada to continue with the construction of that pipe line. If the company decides it will dig into its quite large resources or the resources of its parent companies and pay back the government loan of $80 million, is there anything to prevent the company deciding that it will then sit tight at Winnipeg and await the decision of the F.P.C. before embarking on the construction of the rest of the line from Winnipeg to the Ontario boundary and from Kapuskasing east? We have had nothing presented to the house to show that there is any firm commitment or agreement with the government signed by the company.
Last night, I think it was, we had a very eloquent speech by the hon. member for

Rosthern (Mr. Tucker). Admittedly it did not have very much to do with the pipe line. It had a great deal to do with Saskatchewan politics. But I remember that in the course of that address he avowed his enthusiasm for a government that had the courage and determination to go ahead in the face of obstacles. Well, it may have. It has a great- deal of courage, I must say, to come before the house with some of the measures it brings before the house. In fact, I have thought sometimes, Mr. Speaker, that people like the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and the leader of this group have perhaps been a little unjust when they have taken these measures so seriously and have perhaps mislaid their sense of humour because to my mind nothing so hilarious as this measure has come before the house. Surely this is another gigantic joke on the Canadian people.
But the hon. member for Rosthern is thrilled by the courage of the government in proceeding with this plan. What alternatives have we before us? As I say, we have no firm commitment that this company will build the rest of the line, and if it chose to reimburse the government for its $80 million it could sit tight at Winnipeg. We have, I think, fairly decisive evidence that the company at least considers that the sale of gas in the United States is an essential feature of its scheme, that otherwise it is not economically sound to bring the pipe line to eastern Canada. That would lead us to suppose that if there is any hold-up in the F.P.C. ruling this company is not going to risk any more of its money. Indeed, it has not risked any yet, but if it should decide to repay the government and risk $80 million there is nothing in their past record to suggest that they would be prepared to go on and risk more until they knew for certain that they were going to get into the United States market.
I suggest to the government, and would suggest to the hon. member for Rosthern if he were here, that if they were really contemplating a bold and courageous action they would do what almost inevitably they are going to be forced to do next year. They would take over the construction of this pipe line under a scheme of their own with an investment of Canadian public funds under public ownership. I think it is much wiser, Mr. Speaker, for people to go face first into a proposition rather than to back into it reluctantly and perhaps find themselves situated in an awkward position when they get there. I would suggest that it is not beyond the capacity of the government to undertake the construction of this pipe line to the eastern Canadian markets, and if it is true-I think it is a debatable point from 67509-2651

all I have been able to read-that eastern Canadian markets will not provide a sound, economic basis for the line then we should make plans ourselves for the export of gas across the border to the important New York area market, usually considered, I believe, the most valuable and profitable market in the United States.
That, I think, would be a bold course for this government to take. The course they are taking now is one of being pushed from pillar to post inch by inch, listening to the advice and to the demands of people whose record, if the matter were not so serious for the Canadian people, would really be sidesplittingly funny because I doubt if ever a company has fallen down so consistently on every one of its agreements. I doubt if there is any company which has been proven so often, time and again, to have miscalculated the propositions that it presented to the government. But our government is extremely benevolent and extremely lenient and is always prepared to give them another chance. Now we are prepared to give them a final and, I hope, last chance, but by all accounts we get from Washington the possibility of the federal power commission bringing in a favourable ruling by April of next year is almost nil. There are enormous and equally powerful interests in the United States who are determined to block that ruling for as long as possible, and even though the federal power commission may in the end permit the Tennessee Gas Transmission Company to import gas from Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, even though they may decide to do so, I cannot see it happening until long after this question of the $80 million and when and how it is to be repaid comes again before the house.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to incorporate a railway company under the name of Grand Falls Central Railway Company Limited which will be a wholly owned subsidiary of the Anglo-New-foundland Development Company, generally known in Newfoundland as the A.N.D. Company, which will carry on the existing railway operations of the A.N.D. Company. This company, when originally incorporated under the Newfoundland Act in 1905, was granted at the time of incorporation special rights pertaining to the operation of a railway. It last year celebrated its 50th anniversary.
The railway was constructed to enable the company to carry on its pulp and paper operations, and there are 22 miles of track servicing the towns of Grand Falls, Windsor, Bishop's Falls and Botwood. The railway, which carries the company's products from the Grand Falls paper mill is used also for the transportation of ore concentrate from Buchan's mines as well as the transportation of miscellaneous goods and passengers.
In addition to the railway itself the company maintains storage and wharf facilities at Botwood. The A.N.D. Company has invested in railway equipment a sum in excess of $2 million, and it is employed as a common carrier of goods. However, it is thought desirable that its operations should be in a separate corporation, owing to the magnitude and diversification of the A.N.D. Company operations. The railway company,

servicing as it does four towns in Newfoundland, has an operational character quite distinct from that of the A.N.D. Company itself. One of the main reasons, therefore, for seeking a special bill to incorporate a railroad company is to separate the rail activities from those of the A.N.D. Company.
In addition, after the company is subjected to federal authority in its railway operations it will be a common carrier, and shippers, including not only the A.N.D. Company but all others at present existing or in the future, will be given the benefit of the Maritime Freight Hates Act. The Maritime Freight Rates Act, chapter 174 of the revised statutes of Canada, arbitrarily grants to industries shipping in and out of the maritime provinces a 20 per cent subsidy on rail movement. The statute was enacted to assist the industrial growth of the maritime provinces of Canada, and by section 12 of the act is applicable to the province of Newfoundland. The act was applied to the province in keeping with the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada.
The A. N. D. Company Railway at the present time is a provincial railway, being owned and operated by a company subject only to provincial authority. The operation of the A. N. D. Company railway by a company incorporated by federal act will subject the railway to federal authority in every regard. Principally, the maintenance and operation of the railway will be subject to the provisions of the Railway Act and the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners. The enactment of this act will bring this railway, which is in many regards public in its scope, within the standard pattern of railway operations found throughout Canada.
There exists somewhat similar circumstances where private railways are subject to federal authority, including in the maritimes Canada and Gulf Terminal Railway, Grand Lake and New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company, Cumberland Railway and Coal Company, Dominion Atlantic Railway, and Sydney and Louisburg Railway. The bill asks for the incorporation of the railway and touches on the following points: The capital stock will be $100,000. It is proposed initially that the railway company will rent the railway from the A. N. D. Company, and accordingly the capital stock of the company need not be great at first.
Its head office will be at Grand Falls, Newfoundland. The issue of securities will be limited to $50,000 per mile. It is not intended at the present time to issue any securities, but if and when the railway company acquires the railroad it is thought this would provide adequate financing.

To hold livestock exhibitions.

To hold exhibitions of livestock, agricultural produce and any other products, goods or services produced on or for a farm, and also to make available its facilities for the purchase or sale of any such livestock or other such agricultural produce, products, goods or services.

I notice that in the previous debate in 1952 the attitude was that this bridge represents an opportunity for increasing the flow of tourists to this country, which in the long run will be of great benefit to us. I might make this observation too, sir. One of the two gentlemen listed as a Canadian provisional director is the ubiquitous Mr. Duncan K. MacTavish, who is connected with almost every effort of this kind. How he manages these jobs along with that big political job of his, I cannot venture to suggest.

bridge would revert to public ownership. X assume it would be jointly owned in equal proportions by the state of New York and whatever authority is designated here in Canada. As is well known, Three Rivers is situated at the very heart of the province of Quebec; it is the largest paper-manufacturing centre in the world, and the development of the whole area is making giant strides. It can be seen that the northern shore of the river, in the centre of Quebec, is above all an industrial area. Indeed, the cities of Three Rivers, Cap de la Madeleine, Shawini-gan, Grand Mere and La Tuque, whose population reaches at least 125,000, are enjoying great prosperity. There can be found diversified industries which were attracted there in the wake of power developments on the St. Maurice river.
Across the river, as pointed out by the mover of the bill, we have the largest agricultural county of the province of Quebec, namely Nicolet county, as well as other equally prosperous cities. Unfortunately there are no means of communication between both shores, except the ferry which has always more than it can carry, at least in the summer months. Therefore, I sincerely believe that hon. members should support the second reading of this bill.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 210, to amend the Canada Grain Act (distribution of box cars).
He said: Mr. Speaker, the principle of this bill is to give to the grain producers what I consider to be a fundamental democratic Canadian right, the right to do business with the firm of their own choice. Other Canadians in every walk of life when wishing to make purchases or sales are free to select the firms of their choice.
Because of the very severe congestion in the marketing of grain producers are able to deliver grain only to an elevator which has space, and space is made available in an elevator only when it receives box cars. The proportion by which box cars are allocated to the various elevators constitutes the proportion of deliveries to those elevators.
I have introduced a similar bill on previous occasions and the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said that it would interfere with the wheat board's buying and assembling of grain; if a rigid allocation were made based on the producers' choice, he said the wheat board would not be able to call out the grades and kinds of grain which were required at the time. Thinking there might be some validity in that argument I have placed the following proviso in this bill:
-provided the Canadian wheat board may order cars loaded at any elevator for the purpose of shipping
(i)	out of condition grain or grain in danger of spoilage;
(ii)	grain of a kind and grade that cannot otherwise be acquired for the purpose of meeting Canadian wheat board sales or other requirements.
Apart from that the bill is exactly the same. The bill will allow producers at a given marketing point to allocate their acreage among the elevator companies at that point. After a certain period had elapsed the acreage would be added up and the railway companies would be required to spot box cars in the same proportion that producers had allocated their acreage among the elevator companies.
I might say that the principle of this bill has the support of the main farm organizations in western Canada. We have had a thorough discussion of this subject in the standing committee on agriculture and colonization last year and two years ago and it became clear, particularly last year, that the wheat pool organizations supported a system of box car allocations based upon the producers' choice. It is true that the suggestions they made took a somewhat different form, but the principle of their proposal is

the same, namely that the producers themselves by way of ballot should be entitled to state the allocation of box cars.
Congestion in the west is still very severe at many if not nearly all marketing points. The highest delivery quota in effect today is, I believe, 6 bushels per acre. Of the some
2,000	marketing points, 15 are on a 2-bushel quota; 530 are on a 3-bushel quota; 533 on a 4-bushel quota; 510 on a 5-bushel quota, and 342 on a 6-bushel quota. In other words one-third of the marketing points today are on a low quota of 3 bushels per acre or less. Certainly at the vast majority of marketing points the elevators are plugged. Farmers are able to deliver grain only when box cars are spotted at the elevators.
This is not a situation brought about solely by large crops, or because of difficult marketing conditions, this is something which has been brought about by changed methods of harvesting and delivering grain. With modern methods of harvesting and delivery of grain to the elevators our farmers are able to deliver their whole crop in a very short space of time. That being the case, congestion is almost certain to be with us, at least for given periods during every crop year. With congestion on a semi-permanent basis, it is clear that some different form of allocation of box cars must be arrived at from the one presently in existence.
As I understand it, box cars today are allocated in this way. The wheat board hands out shipping orders to the various elevator companies and at' various marketing points. The transport controller then may or may not discuss with the railway companies the overall total of box cars that' must be made available within a given period of time, but when it comes to the actual number of box cars placed at' a given elevator it is the responsibility of the railway company.
So the railway companies themselves are actually allocating the box cars as among elevators. Some elevator companies may complain of the distribution on the grounds that their company is receiving an unfair allocation of box cars. I am not particularly interested in whether a given elevator company claims it is getting fewer box cars than it is entitled to, but I am interested in establishing the principle that a producer shall have the right to deliver grain to the elevator of his choice.
I see no reason why the railway companies, instead of the producers, should be given the right to allocate box cars and to determine the number of box cars that will go to a given elevator company at a given point. If you have four elevator companies at a given point 67509-266
Canada Grain Act
and it should happen that the railway companies spot box cars on an absolutely equal basis, one car for each elevator, that is precisely the allocation of the grain the farmers must make. If the railway company, for one reason or another, should spot twice as many box cars at one elevator as it does at some other elevator, the farmers must under the circumstances deliver twice as much grain to the elevator getting twice as many box cars.
We heard a great deal of evidence on this subject a year ago. We had some evidence two years ago, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that he was actively considering-and I took it to mean that he was going to establish-a system of box car cycles based on past experiences, with allocation at a given marketing point determined on a certain base period. The car cycle was never established.
Last year, before the agriculture committee, we had representatives from farm organizations, in particular representatives from the farmers' union and the wheat pools, speaking in favour of the principle of giving to the farmers once a year a chance to state where they wished to deliver their grain. On the basis of the statements of the producers, those instructions should go out to the railway companies to so apportion box cars. That has not been adopted. The government has said no.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this bill. I had not intended to get into the debate at this stage, but in view of the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia I think I particularly, as chairman of the agriculture committee, should say a few words on what faced us there.
This is the first time I have heard him refer to the committee report last year as a whitewash of government policy. I realize that the government members have a majority on that committee, but in all fairness I think other members, even from other parties, will agree with me that in our consideration of this matter last year we went to very great lengths and considered all angles of the problem. I am sure that many members of other parties will agree that we came to one conclusion. I am not referring to the report; I am referring to the minds of the members who heard all the evidence that was presented.
I think we will all agree, and we have to admit, that in the circumstances in which the Canadian wheat board and the board of grain commissioners are operating at the present time, and were operating last year, the one over-all and primary consideration that has to be kept in mind is that the grain has to be made available and brought in to a selling position, and that has to override any other consideration. To be able to do that, it was recognized by all that we had to give priority
"Mr. Argue.]
to the Canadian wheat board, and the right to proceed on the basis of shipping orders.
As I say, one of the important things is to get the grain in a position where we shall be able to deliver it when people ask to purchase grain from the Canadian wheat board. If we start from the assumption that shipping orders have a priority over everything else, then there is not much practical point in inserting new sections in the Canada Grain Act or putting in new provisions, because even these will have to take second place to the shipping orders of the Canadian wheat board. In effect you only add a new clause to an act, which clause cannot be operative under the circumstances. We went into this matter at very great length and came to the conclusion, which was an honest one, that in view of this over-all priority the best that could be done in the circumstances was to make sure that box cars would be spotted in the same proportion as the shipping orders issued by the Canadian wheat board.
The hon. member for Assiniboia made the statement a while ago that the railways were allocating the box cars. That statement is not quite accurate. It is true, and it is bound to be true, that the railways spot the cars. I do not think anybody would suggest that people from the Canadian wheat board should go out to all the stations and spot the cars. The spotting is done on instructions of the Canadian wheat board or the transport controller, and it has already been placed on the record that the railways have been instructed to spot the cars in proportion to the shipping orders issued by the Canadian wheat board, as was recommended by the standing committee on agriculture last year. I see the hon. member for Assiniboia shaking his head.

The claim is made by the hon. member that the railways are not doing that. My information is that they are, at least to a great degree. I should add here on this point that all last fall, all last year as a matter of fact, because of the unusual congestion period, possibly the worst, through which we went, I doubt if any wholly satisfactory system could have been devised and put into operation. For several months until winter there was no movement at all with the exception of malting barley, flax and grain in demand by the domestic millers of the country. As we know, Canadian millers, as is the case everywhere else but particularly in Canada, want special grades of grain from particular localities according to the protein content of that grain. Therefore when you have demands affecting special areas and only special areas, there is no system of allocation of box cars you can possibly institute

that will spread box cars all over the three western provinces. These are very exceptional cases.
To try to judge at this time the attempt made last year as the result of the recommendation of the committee is, I think, premature because I do not think there has been sufficient time to put the plan into operation properly. I am informed that within the last few months another attempt has been made. I believe the railway agents have been asked to post the shipping orders of the various companies in their localities. Once they do that they give a clear indication to the various elevator houses at the particular point as to exactly what the Canadian wheat board shipping orders are. Thus the various companies are able to check and see whether this particular instruction about which I am talking, the spotting of box cars in proportion to shipping orders, is being carried out, and will be in a position to state definitely whether or not the railways are complying with the orders.
I have no doubt that once this system is in general use box cars will be spotted in accordance with the instructions issued by the transport controller. As we know, the railway companies as a whole are not there to make the situation more difficult. They are usually quite co-operative. They are quite prepared to do what is feasible and practical from their point of view. The only thing is that they want to know definitely what they are supposed to do before attempting to do it. With this latest development I have no doubt that box cars will be spotted in the same proportion as shipping orders are issued.
But the allocation of box cars and the actual sale of grain are, of course, two different things altogether. No matter what you do by way of allocating box cars it does not add to the number of box cars and does not add to the deliveries that are to be made. I must come back again to the point which was made in another debate. The hon. member for Assiniboia is very insistent with respect to the question of the 3-bushel quota or the 2-bushel quota or the 1 or the 5. I want to submit again that the quota does not tell the whole story. As I said previously, even with a higher quota in Manitoba our wheat deliveries for this crop year are below the average of the last ten years. Therefore the actual quota does not tell the whole story. What tells the whole story is the actual amount of grain that is delivered, and I submit that it is not right merely to take the quota if you want to make a fair comparison between districts or between provinces.
For instance, there may be a 5-bushel quota and not enough grain to deliver more 67509-266J

They already had an elevator and they built two annexes. Naturally with 5 and 8-bushel quotas they have practically enough space to take care of the whole crop. But to point to this situation and say that this is unfair to farmers in Saskatchewan or Alberta is to give an entirely wrong impression.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION OF CROWN COMPANY TO CONSTRUCT PIPE LINE, MAKE SHORTTERM LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose this evening to deal with one particular aspect of this pipe-line controversy. I should like to discuss public versus private ownership. The C.C.F. group in this debate, in accordance with its principles, has advocated public ownership and has moved an appropriate amendment. I think the house and taxpayers generally should realize that if this amendment carries, the taxpayers of Canada ultimately will probably have to find in the neighbourhood of $1 billion in investment funds.
The government, on the other hand, has suggested that it will build the pipe line by public ownership, only as a last resort. In trying to assess the relative merits of the two methods of ownership, it seems to me that hon. members might benefit from the experience of the Saskatchewan government since 1944 in experimenting with state ownership.

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation
Twelve years ago, in an effort to diversify our economy and provide jobs for Saskatchewan citizens, the C.C.F. government embarked on a program of state ownership. They introduced a program of socialized industry. I think the objectives of the program were laudable. Certainly most people at that time were sympathetic with those objectives.
But in this pipe-line debate, where one of the major issues is public ownership, I suggest that two questions should be posed and considered. First, in Saskatchewan have publicly-owned companies been able to operate efficiently? Second, has the experiment as a whole been successful? I think the answers to those questions should be of value in these deliberations.
Now, Mr. Speaker, since taking office in 1944 the C.C.F. government has either laken over or set up 19 different crown corporations. In those companies it has invested the sum of approximately $130 million. I suggest we take a look at each company individually to see how it has fared. One of the first enterprises set up was a leather tannery. The purpose of the industry was to tan Saskatchewan hides and make them into leather. Unfortunately its activities were ill-fated and short-lived. The company moved from one economic crisis to another until 1952. In that year it was leased to a private company, but only after the venture had cost the taxpayers of my province, in operating deficits, about $260,000.
A shoe factory was set up in 1945 to utilize the leather which was made in the tanning factory. I recall that Premier Douglas, speaking in Brandon, Manitoba, announced, and I quote from his speech:
The tannery and shoe factory, now being operated by the C.C.F., can make shoes for $2.75 a pair and not lose money.
In spite of the premier's optimism on that occasion the shoe factory did lose money. So much so, in fact, that in 1948 it closed down after having accumulated deficits of more than $82,000.
A housing corporation was set up after the war to convert military huts into housing accommodation which could be rented. Despite the fact that its progress in building housing accommodation was extremely limited, after a very few months it was able to accumulate a deficit of $42,400. In 1947 this corporation closed down.
Very early in its first term of office the C.C.F. government set up a fish board and built a number of fish filleting plants in northern Saskatchewan for the purpose of helping northern fishermen. Every commercial fisherman in the province was compelled by law to
(Mr. Thatcher.]
sell his fish to the board. Despite this fact, almost from its inception the board lost money. After accumulating a deficit of roughly $400,000, the government was forced to close it down in 1949. The fish board was then replaced by the fish marketing service which was given annual grants by the government. This new service, up to the end of last year, had accumulated deficits of $180,000.
A woollen mill was set up in my home city of Moose Jaw. It was intended as a method of utilizing Saskatchewan wool. The theory behind it was excellent. This industry, however, was in difficulties from its opening day, and when it finally was forced to close in 1951 it had accumulated deficits of $830,000, and had paid no interest at all on its advances. The mill was transferred to a private company at bargain basement prices. That company finally moved the machinery out of the province, and today the whole operation is defunct.
In 1951 a lumber mill was set up at Big Beaver, Saskatchewan. Within a year and a half the mill had an operating deficit of almost $100,000, and had cost the treasury another $54,000 in interest on its advances. In 1951 the mill was merged with the provincial timber board, and since that time its losses have been concealed and absorbed by the board.
A brick plant was set up in the town of Estevan. From its incorporation that plant has run into engineering difficulties, technical difficulties, selling difficulties, overproduction; and high employee lay-offs. As a matter of fact, in nine years of operation the government sank $900,000 into the venture, which managed to pile up a deficit of $176,000 by the end of last year.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in every one of the cases I have mentioned so far there was competition from private enterprise. It is significant to note that under those circumstances, in virtually every case the crown corporation was unable to compete effectively. Invariably they lost money, and usually they were forced to close their doors completely.
What of the other crown corporations? Superficially some of them have shown substantial profits, but again without exception, closer examination and analysis shows that they were able to do so because they enjoyed either government compulsion or some kind of monopoly privileges. The Saskatchewan telephone company is a very good example. Hon. members will realize that in Saskatchewan the telephone business is a complete monopoly. Since the end of the war the company has increased its rates numerous times, and very steeply. As a result the government

has been able to show a profit of $3-8 million. In other words the crown corporation-

I will tell the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) that experience is a great teacher, and it is a very foolish man who will not benefit from experience.
Another two crown corporations which were set up were the Saskatchewan government insurance office and Saskatchewan Guarantee and Fidelity Limited. Last year these companies showed a combined profit of $460,000. At first glance this is very gratifying. However, when you examine the companies you find that much of the business has been obtained by compulsion. For instance, every person in Saskatchewan today who wants to licence his car or his truck, must at the same time take out an insurance policy from the government insurance office. There is another law which is equally interesting. This law says that every hospital, every sanatorium, university, every school or every orphanage which receives a grant from the provincial government, must take out its insurance with the Saskatchewan government insurance office. So I say it is small wonder that under those circumstances these companies can show a profit.
A printing company was set up by the provincial government, which over the years has accumulated profits of $470,000. Of course, I am very gratified that it has been able to make these profits. But once again it should be realized that the company enjoys a monopoly of government printing. There is no such thing as competition. It sets its own rates.
A sodium sulphate plant was set up in the town of Chaplin. Several private companies were already operating throughout the province at the time, but the government regulations were passed which either forced these companies out of business, or forced them to sell to the provincial government. One such plant was in my old riding of Moose Jaw at Bishopric. I say that as a result of the un-fairest kind of competition that plant at Chaplin has been able to show a surplus.
The Saskatchewan timber board is one of the most profitable of all crown corporations. Up to the end of last year it had accumulated profits of $2-8 million. How did it do so? Because it has a complete monopoly of all the lumber harvested in the province of Saskatchewan. Every person is forced to sell his lumber to the timber board at relatively low prices. Then the government, in turn, sells the lumber on the high Canadian and United States markets.
The government has a fur marketing board, and at the end of 1955 that fur marketing
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation board had accumulated a surplus of $346,000. Once again the reason is apparent. Every trapper in Saskatchewan, until recently, was forced by law to sell his skins to the fur marketing board.	,
A bus company was set up and it was given a monopoly of all the major routes within the province. Any companies which were then operating in the province were forced to sell out to the provincial monopoly. Despite that monopoly, last year this bus company on an investment of $1,900,000 was only able to make a nominal profit of $12,000, and if proper accounting methods had been used it would have lost money.
Now I wish to say a word about the Saskatchewan power commission, which distributes electricity, but which also has set up a gas monopoly quite recently in my province. I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough) the other day, and on page 4096 of Hansard he is reported as having made this statement:
I, together with my colleagues in the C.C.F. party, feel it is essential that this be a public undertaking, so the Canadian consumers of gas will not be fleeced by a monopoly in that field.
I suggest that we look at comparative rates for a moment to see what company is doing the fleecing. Today in Edmonton, which is roughly the same distance from the gas field as my home city of Moose Jaw, the domestic rate averages 29 cents. I am told that the Calgary rate is 30 cents, and in all the Alberta cities the rate is roughly comparable.
In Saskatchewan the C.C.F. government is charging 83 cents in the city of Saskatoon and it is proposing to charge a similar price in Moose Jaw and Regina. I say that such a price looks fantastically high to me. Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, the company we are discussing today, proposes to deliver gas in the province of Saskatchewan for 21-3 cents per thousand cubic feet, at 100 per cent load factor. In Manitoba they will deliver gas at 26-2 cents.
I admit at once that the cost of distribution would be over and above these figures. But I have discussed this matter with the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Nickle), and he informed me that the average cost of distribution in Alberta cities is 15 cents. In other words, I say that the government monopoly in the gas field in the province of Saskatchewan is charging more than double what private enterprise is charging in the province of Alberta.
I say that if any company is doing any fleecing in the gas industry today, it is the Saskatchewan power commission in my province. I also say, Mr. Speaker, that if such

I say tonight, Mr. Speaker, that the Saskatchewan program of socialization was born in high hopes and with laudable aspirations. But today it is apparent that the program has bogged down in a morass of bungling, red tape, inefficiency and inexperience. I say there is not a single Saskatchewan crown corporation that has operated in the black for a reasonable length of time without special privileges or compulsion of some kind. I say the program has been a tragedy and a very costly fiasco. I think it has been a dismal failure. At one time I believed in public ownership. Pipe Line Filibustering Should Arouse Suspicion
In the squabble over the Trans-Canada pipe line proposal, it should not be forgotten that it was Premier Leslie Frost, who, years ago, took a lead in the proposal to bring Alberta natural gas to eastern Canada, and particularly to his own province of Ontario.
From that beginning, the Trans-Canada project has gradually developed to the stage where, with a reasonable amount of support, the line is apt to be built and Alberta gas is likely to be delivered to Ontario consumers.
It is at this critical stage of the project that we first find public men whose attitude, not so long ago, was one of benevolent neutrality, now vehemently assailing the project.
It is at this critical stage that we begin to hear of rival promoters who are prepared-on paper or over the air-to do this and that.
The suspicion will not down that the purpose of the sudden last minute flurry of political activity, the deluge of propaganda and the alluring "alternative offers" is, not to work out a better policy but to serve political ends-and to keep Alberta gas out of Ontario.
In particular, the proposal the McMahon interests made, or are reported to have made, has all the earmarks of a dog-in-the-manger proposition; perhaps an attempt to delay the Trans-Canada enterprise till the McMahon interests have piped the lion's share of the gas to American markets.

speechtext:
In my opinion the failure of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines to live up to its definite and specific promises has caused the government considerable internal embarrassment and during recent days much external embarrassment, and has caused them to present this most unpalatable legislative nostrum to the house at this time. I have read the speech of the Minister of Finance yesterday carefully, and having watched his manner of delivery and his expression it would indicate to me that the government had not taken the plunge into the ice cold water of nation-wide criticism until after a lot of consideration, and with some hesitation and I believe even some doubts at the present time as to the course they are pursuing.
We oppose the bill, Mr. Speaker, because we believe the public interest would be best served by public ownership of the pipe line as a national transportation utility. Since this question was first mooted in the house some five or six years ago C.C.F. conventions, the C.C.F. national council and C.C.F. members of the house have consistently urged three things in particular in connection with this type of legislation. The first was the public ownership of a trans-Canada pipe line. The second was an all-Canadian route, and the third was the assured protection of Canadian consumers' interests and their future needs. All that is provided by the present pipe-line legislation is an all-Canadian route.
The record of Hansard, the record of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, the debates in the house on various bills and legislation and votes taken on various amendments all indicate the consistent advocacy by this group of the three things I have mentioned. I want to compare that consistent approach throughout the years with the record of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, and I should like to quote now from the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines for March 6, 1951, at page 10. This is what I read in the evidence:
The second consideration was that it should be an all-Canadian project, that it would be
4202	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation Canadian gas transported over a Canadian line, and that 100 per cent of the consumption would be in Canadian cities.
Who made that statement? That statement was made by Mr. Frank A. Schultz, vicepresident of the parent company. Other expert witnesses testified before the committee that the pipe line could be constructed on this basis, and it was on this basis that parliament finally gave the bill third reading on March 9, 1951.
To indicate how assured the government was in this matter and the government's confidence in the sponsors, on February 27, 1951, as recorded at page 735 of Hansard, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) said:
All consumers will be in Canada. No gas will be exported out of Canada.
At that time, Mr. Speaker, no mention was made by the company that it would need financial assistance from the government. No mention was made of the necessity to export gas to the United States in order to make the operation sound. In the bill now before us the government is presenting an entirely different proposal.
What does it mean to Canada? I think this is a most important piece of legislation. I think there is some indication of what it means to Canada in the attitude and efforts of the opposition on this side of the house to prevent the legislation being passed. Another indication is the comments of editors all across the country. We must remember that these Liberal, Conservative and independent editors of these newspapers are close to the people, and when they write editorials they have their ears to the ground. In many cases they are writing what they think is the opinion of the people of the district in which their papers are published. We find, as I said, that Liberal, Conservative and independent newspapers across the country are criticizing this proposal in no uncertain terms.
I want to refer at this point to some remarks made yesterday by the Minister of Finance. I am glad to see that he is listening. He is a good listener. He held out as another bait the enormous amount of taxation the exchequer would receive. He said that 45 per cent to 50 per cent of the total profits would accrue to the treasury of this country, and he indicated that it would be a very large sum because he hinted it would be possible to do very big things with the money. We in this group believe that when the people provide the risk capital they should get all the profits, and not 45 or 50 per cent of them.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, we maintain that public ownership of the pipe line is to the great advantage of all Canadians, and on
LMr. Herridge.]

this foundation the C.C.F. rests its case in this debate. However, in this connection it is interesting to note that the accounting firm of Clarkson, Gordon and Company of Toronto, appointed by the Ontario government to look into the economics of the whole gas pipe line, declared in their report:
An all government owned pipe line would be economically feasible, even though no sales were made to the United States.
We are not saying that, but that is a prominent economist who says it after making a survey of this pipe line.
What are the advantages of public ownership of this pipe line? From our point of view they are these: The government can raise money cheaper than private enterprise. This was indicated again this afternoon when the Prime Minister was speaking. Second, no income or sales taxes need apply. Third, the government can amortize the scheme for this pipe line over a period of 40 years, whereas under private ownership it is usual to amortize a scheme of this sort over 20 years. Fourth, the annual carrying charges on a publicly-owned line are estimated by economists as from 6 per cent to 7 per cent, whereas on a privately-owned line they are from 13 per cent to 14 per cent. I suggest that the consumers of gas will pay for that difference. The last and very particular reason that there is advantage in public ownership is that the protection of Canadian consumers' interests is guaranteed, for the present and in the future.
In that connection, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer particularly to some remarks made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). You will remember that he said that the producers in Alberta, that is the United States corporations, are opposed to public ownership of this pipe line. He indicated in general terms that the reason was that there are far more consumers of gas in Canada than there are producers of gas, and therefore a government-owned pipe line would naturally have to give consideration to the larger number, that is the Canadian consumers. They would have to consider the people first before the interests of the corporation. I think, Mr. Speaker, that is an excellent argument in favour of public ownership.
I want to make a few more references, but I find it very difficult to condense a speech. I have been sitting here for the last two or three days with a 30 or 40-minute speech prepared and I have to kiln dry it, as they say in the lumber industry. I want to refer to some remarks made by the hon. member for Calgary South. He said he deeply regretted that some had chosen to

inject various elements of emotionalism. I find that the dictionary definition of emotion is feeling, passion, mental agitation or sentiment. I trust that the Canadian people will never lose emotion, sentiment or feeling. You do not find those things in corporations, you find them in human beings.
Canadian history is replete with examples of Canadians being stirred to action to defend the national interest by emotions, by sentiment and by feeling for this country. In the war of 1812, which I consider as the watershed of our national history, the French Canadians of this country fought valiantly to defend it, and why? Because they had a feeling for Canada. The first shot of the civil war in the United States was fired on April 12, 1861. This first shot created the national emotion, sentiment and feeling that finally brought about confederation in Canada in 1867. In world wars I and II the same emotion, the same sentiment, the same feeling for Canada that the hon. member regrets caused hundreds of thousands of men in this country to volunteer their services in its defence.
In that connection I want to quote briefly from Bruce Hutchison's book "Struggle for the Border", page 489. He said:
A vague but undeniable force called "Canadian-ism" for lack of a better word, bestrides the upper slope of America. Inarticulate, puzzled, amorphous, incalculable in its outcome, with no visible limits to its future.
Then on page 488 he says:
If the twentieth century does not belong to Canada, or indeed to any state or group of states, Canada clearly belongs to Canadians.
We in this group support that sentiment, that feeling and that emotion. Nations are not built in the brokerage shops and counting houses of the oil and gas businesses. They are built in the hearts of the Canadian people whose emotions, feelings and sentiments call us to rise in defence of this country when the occasion requires.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what are our financial resources? Some may say it is not possible for the government to undertake this project. I find on reference to the Bank of Canada statistical summary that in December, 1955, we had $10,848 million in bank deposits by federal and provincial governments, corporations or individuals. Surely we know what Canadians are like. We have the human and we have the financial resources to build this pipe line at this time. We therefore urge the minister to allow this bill to go to a committee. This afternoon a bill was allowed to go to a committee to consider only a change in name, but this important matter is not going to be considered by a committee if the minister can
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation avoid it. The minister should sponsor public ownership and this bill should be sent to the committee.
We in this group suggest this project should be financed by an issue of national development bonds in denominations which would make it possible for all Canadians to participate in public investment to their mutual advantage. Special issues could be floated for the trans-Canada pipe line, Mica creek, the South Saskatchewan dam and power development in the maritimes. We are confident the response to such an appeal would confirm the desire of Canadians for the public ownership of these projects by Canadians. With a hard-working and progressive population, and nearly $11,000 million on deposit in our banks, it is evident we have the human and financial resources to undertake this project satisfactorily. All that is required is the will and the leadership of this government.
