Mr. Speaker, I wish first to deal with something the hon. member for Prince Albert had to say about me when he participated in this debate last Thursday. At page 4032 of Hansard for May 17, 1956, the hon. member referred to three cabinet ministers by saying that they have one kind of speech in parliament and when they go down to the province of Quebec they change their attitude as they campaign in provincial elections. The hon. member then mentioned the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) and myself.
I wish to say first of all, sir, that I have not dealt with this question in the house yet in this debate, and second that I have made only two political speeches in the present campaign in Quebec. I have discussed neither foreign investment in Canada nor control over natural resources. My colleagues the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Minister of Transport have assured me that they have not dealt with these questions. It is true
4204	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation that the Liberal leader in Quebec, Mr. La-palme, has criticized the government of the Union Nationale for its policy on the use and control of the natural resources, especially iron ore; but Mr. Lapalme has said publicly also that he favours foreign investment in Canada for the development of the natural resources of Canada and of Quebec in particular. As a matter of fact, when I myself heard the Quebec Liberal leader criticize the administration of the Union Nationale with regard to the exploitation of Ungava iron ore, he gave as an example of the policy he thought Quebec should follow the policy that has been followed in Alberta in the management of the oil and gas resources of that province.
It is clear, sir-it seems clear to me-that the hon. member for Prince Albert, along with other opposition members, and I could mention the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), this afternoon, and the hon. member for York West (Mr. Hamilton) tonight, are doing their best to try to blur and confuse the issue which is before this house. There is a clear distinction between foreign investment on the one hand, and on the other hand the use of and control over natural resources in Canada. The fact that a majority of the stock of a Canadian company is held by foreign interests does not transfer to that company the control over the natural resources which it exploits.
In dealing shortly with the question of financial ownership and control, I wish first to refer to the comparison which has been made with the manner in which things were handled in the good old days when the Canadian Pacific Railway was built. I have not been able to find any figures for 1881, the year in which the Canadian Pacific Railway was founded. In 1883, however, 290,000 shares out of a total of 550,000, which means more than half, were held in New York state. It was only somewhat later than this that the large volume of British capital entered the picture.
I could not secure the figures for 1885, the year when the railway was completed. I can, however, give the proportion of voting stock which was held in various countries in 1915. In 1915 Canada held 13-6 per cent; the United Kingdom and other commonwealth countries held 62-9 per cent, and the United States held 10-4 per cent. Other countries held 14-1 per cent.
In 1936 Canada's holding of the voting stock had fallen to 11-4 per cent; the United Kingdom and other commonwealth countries had risen to 65-6 per cent; and the United States holding to 17-6 per cent, leaving 6-4 per cent in the hands of other countries.


From then on there was a strong shift in the holdings as between the United Kingdom and the United States, but Canada's position changed only slightly. In December, 1954, that is a year and a half ago, residents of Canada held 12-2 per cent; residents of the United Kingdom and other British countries held 46-3 per cent; residents of the United States held 34 [DOT] 4 per cent, and other countries held 8-1 per cent. Never, therefore, as far as I can ascertain, have Canadians held more than about one-eighth of the voting stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
I would ask hon. members to compare this situation with the agreement that Trans-Canada has made to offer 51 per cent of its common shares in Canada, and that it intends to effect a wide distribution of those shares throughout Canada. Any amount of sneering at this agreement as a "shallow pretence" does not take away from the fact that it has been made, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said, as a solemn covenant.
What other steps did Sir John A. Macdonald take to see that control of the Canadian Pacific Railway remained in Canada? The only other step was a provision in the railway's articles of incorporation that a majority of the board of directors should be British subjects. There was, of course, no such thing as Canadian citizenship in those days. However, a provision could have been inserted that the majority of the directors should be British subjects residing in Canada; but no such provision was in fact inserted. If we look at the original board of 1881, we find that it consisted of the following people: George Stephen and Duncan McIntyre, president and vice president, both of whom were Canadians; R. B. Angus, a Scotsman who was living in St. Paul, Minnesota when he was appointed but who spent much of his life in Canada; J. J. Hill, Canadian-born, who spent most of his business career in the United States and who was living in St. Paul when appointed; J. S. Kennedy, of New York; Baron J. de Reinach, of Paris; H. S. Northcote, of London, of the Hudson's Bay Company; P. duP. Grenfell, of London; and Sir John Rose, who had been minister of finance in Canada but had returned to London. However, sir, the point I wish to make is that under the law there was nothing at all to prevent all the directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway from being British subjects living in London, who had never set foot in Canada.
How does this situation compare with the requirements in respect of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines? As hon. members know, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines was incorporated by special act

of parliament under the Canadian Companies Act. The learned lawyers who sit in front of me now seem to have forgotten section 155 of the Companies Act, which applies to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, and I wish to quote it to hon. members:
No person shall be elected as a director unless he is a shareholder owning shares absolutely in his own right, and not in arrear in respect of any call thereon; and the majority of the directors of the company so chosen shall, at all times, be persons resident in Canada, and subjects of Her Majesty, by birth or naturalization.
Far more effective steps, therefore, are taken in the case of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines to ensure that Canadians have a share in the management of the company than was ever done in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Oh, I know, of course, that some of my hon. friends like to maintain that the fact that it was British capital rather than United States capital which built the Canadian Pacific Railway made a great deal of difference. I agree that it might have made a lot of difference, but I am not sure it is in the way they suggest. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, in reply to a question by the Minister of Justice, agreed that the bulk of investment in the Canadian Pacific Railway came from the United Kingdom, but he pointed out that Canada at that time was a dominion within the British commonwealth. He further pointed out that Canada is not now a dominion, nor is it a nation within the North American union of the United States, which is all correct. He implied that it was quite harmless for Canadian resources to be developed by British interests in our colonial days, but that it would be disastrous today for our resources to be developed by United States capital.
To me, sir, it seems that the hon. gentleman's argument should be turned around. It is, as you say, topsy-turvy. In the days when Canada was to a substantial degree under the control of Great Britain, the development of Canadian resources by British interests could entail the risk of both economic and political dependence. But today Canada is an independent nation, and we certainly can accept the foreign capital that we need for the development of our resources without endangering our independence or our sovereignty, just as the United States did 100 years ago.
This brings me to the final point I wish to make. I cannot understand how people can claim that the development of Canadian resources by Canadian companies when financed for the majority of their stock in the United States can represent United States control over Canadian resources. There is a difference between foreign investment and
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation control over resources. In the first place, a Canadian company engaged in developing natural resources in Canada will tend to act in certain ways under certain circumstances, and will act in that fashion irrespective of whether or not the ownership of the company is in the majority Canadian or American. Moreover, natural resources which are developed by private companies are not in any real sense of the word controlled by those companies. The development of these resources is controlled by the whole complex of laws which have been passed by the federal and provincial governments of Canada.
Precisely what this complex of laws comprises depends upon the subject in question but what I have in mind is, for instance, the Companies Act, tax legislation, anti-combine legislation, labour legislation, tariff legislation and specific legislation referring to the development of the natural resource in question,
Surely, sir, Canada's governments, federal and provincial, have reached the stage of development where they can see to it that foreign investment does not develop our natural resources in a manner which is harmful to Canada's interests, and it is to ensure that Alberta natural gas will be used and developed in the interests of Canada first that we are now studying this legislation.
Surely, sir, we have now reached the point in our political development where we can accept all the assistance in developing our natural resources which may be offered by foreign capital, and yet manage without any difficulty whatsoever to keep control of these resources in our own hands.

I am very glad to have the opportunity of taking part in this discussion and expressing several convictions with respect to the subject before us. May I begin by saying that I have listened intently to the various speeches that have been made by those members who have participated in this debate. Whilst I do not question the sincerity of their views, which are different from my own, it has been for me a most dismal disappointment to find so little substance in the arguments that have been used against this proposition, a proposition which should mean the undertaking of one of the great engineering feat's of our time, with immeasurable benefits to all Canada, namely the building of the trans-Canada pipe line from my native province of Alberta to the eastern provinces.
Sir, I respect every person's opinion provided it is honest and based on fact, but with the exception of creating a great deal of apprehension and doubt in the minds of the Canadian people, with the exception of giving a black eye to a vital industry, with the exception of doing great disservice to outside investors who have come to our country and made sizeable investments generously and in good faith, neither the C.C.F. nor the Conservatives have suggested one single alternative that is acceptable to this house and that would ensure the building of a natural gas pipe line to be completed by the end of this year. That is the real issue before us at this time. To continue stalling is to do irreparable harm to the economy of my province and foul up this project beyond any hope of repair.
I can appreciate the position of the C.C.F. in this debate. As usual they are taking the stand of advocating their pet doctrine of state ownership, state control and state monopoly-"the state is boss"-but for the Conservative members, members of that once

great, proud and independent party which professes to be the champion of private enterprise, to be outmanoeuvred and led into the camp of the C.C.F., from which they are imposing further impediments in the way of private enterprise, is, to say the least shockingly sad. Surely they must understand that what they are doing is destroying little by little the last potential for private enterprise to undertake this pipe line and make it a success.
With each of the Social Credit members, my colleagues, I share a deep feeling of responsibility in taking part in this debate and expressing views on a matter which is as crucial to Alberta's and Canada's welfare as this issue before us. It is with such a sense of responsibility that we have placed politics aside and appraised this question strictly on its merits.
When one considers the fundamental point there is only one thing that can be done. There is no other course but to accept or reject this proposition. To deny this proposition at this time is to make certain that no pipe line will be built in the foreseeable future, for no other company than Trans-Canada Pipe Lines has spent $8 million or so of its capital in preparatory work, in surveying and acquiring rights of way. No company but Trans-Canada has, ordered and ready, the 34-inch diameter pipe required for the western portion of this line. No other company is prepared to call for tenders in order that machines and men can proceed with the job as quickly as possible.

This expansion program has been stimulated by the atmosphere of good governments, and the reputation of this country for fair dealing has encouraged outside capital and personnel to be directed to Canada. The Canadian reputation to which I refer can best be described in the words of Hon. Leslie Frost, premier of Ontario, in a debate in the Ontario legislature on February 21, 1956, as reported at page 392 of Ontario legislature Hansard:
Do not regard the fact that money comes here in large quantities as any deterrent. That is what has made and will make the wheels go around. This afternoon the Prime Minister said he intended to devote part of his time to closure and part to the bill itself. As a matter of fact I think he divided his time about equally between the two matters. The hon. member for Kamloops replied, and also referred to closure. The Minister of Justice said he spent about 90 per cent of his time on things other than the bill, and I think he was quite justified in doing that.
What is the situation with respect to closure? It is something which has been grafted upon our rules in very recent days, from a historical standpoint. Closure was a practice which developed in continental European parliaments, where they were riven with groups and divisions of all sorts and where certain groups were determined to obstruct parliament. Closure, or the old French word cloture, was first defined and incorporated in the rules in Britain during the days when the Irish nationalist group attempted to obstruct parliament in order to so nullify the actions of parliament that the British parliament, perhaps in disgust, would grant them Irish home rule; that is when it came to Britain. We adopted it later.
I venture to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that no parliament in the British commonwealth, leaving aside for a moment the British parliament itself, has ever adopted closure except after a long and protracted debate on the various stages of the bill. It is, as the Prime Minister suggested this afternoon, something which you reluctantly grasp; it is something with which you reluctantly deal, and why? Because it is a gag which nullifies parliament.
Never in the history of a parliament in the British commonwealth have we reached the stage which we have now reached in this parliament, where in the opening speech at the resolution stage the right hon. gentleman who speaks first says, "Parliament, you are through; I am giving notice that this debate concludes tomorrow night at one o'clock". It is true that closure was adopted in 1913; it is true that it was adopted in 1917 and sometime in 1926 and in 1932. You can count the number of times on the fingers of one hand. But never in this country or any other country has it been adopted during the preliminary stage as it was here.
There is one question we would like to have answered. Why it was done at that 

time? If you are going to introduce closure at the resolution stage, why summon parliament? You are negativing the whole procedure. As the hon. member for Kamloops pointed out very effectively this afternoon, the resolution stage is the most effective stage at which debate and inquiry can be conducted.
It is interwoven in our constitution that when a bill involving the expenditure of money is brought before the house it should be preceded by a resolution. Why? Because in the old days the king had to justify to parliament why it was even necessary to bring in a bill, and until that justification had been established the bill could not be introduced. In this case the resolution is introduced one day and debate finishes the next. As I said, it is a negation of parliament. It is now going to serve as a precedent because, since it has been done on this bill, it can be done again on some other bill.
This is the most important bill which has been before the House of Commons for 25 years, at any rate, and perhaps 50 years, and debate is precluded. Why do you not close up this place? The Minister of Trade and Commerce has not made a very successful job of selling wheat. Perhaps we could use this building more effectively to store wheat, rather than have a nullified debate such as we have now.
I read the speech the right hon. gentleman made at a meeting in the Chateau Laurier on the occasion of a birthday party, or a celebration of some kind, in that building in January or February, and he said: "I am afraid, like Churchill, that I am a House of Commons man". Well, Mr. Speaker, he does not have to be very much afraid. He is the only one that is afraid of it, I can tell you that, because Churchill suffered a lot of criticism and abuse but I do not think he ever had to stand a body blow like this. Anyone who introduces closure at the opening stage of a debate and then says, "I am a House of Commons man" is using his imagination.
Tonight we are on the second reading of the bill. It is now a quarter after eleven. An hour and 45 minutes from now, unless someone happens to have the floor for a few moments, this debate will be concluded and the guillotine will fall. This is the second reading of the bill, the time at which we are supposed to discuss the principle of the bill.

This building program will involve the expenditure of many millions


of dollars in Canada. In addition, the knowledge that the pipe line exists will stimulate further exploration for potential gas sources and the development of those sources when found. This means more dollars spent in Canada. At the other end of the line, in Ontario and Quebec, large capital and maintenance investments will have to be made in the manufacture of equipment for the distribution of the gas. Hence there will be increased industrial activity, increased employment, increased national income.
The years since the second world war have been years of expansion in Canada on a scale so tremendous that if anyone had seriously predicted them two decades ago he would have been dismissed out of hand as an eggheaded visionary. We have had the expansion of the aluminum industry at Kitimat, the expansion of the iron ore industry at Steep Rock and in Labrador, the expansion of hydroelectric power facilities in Ontario and Quebec, the expansion of transportation facilities through the St. Lawrence seaway, the expansion of atomic energy facilities at Chalk River. And now we are on the threshold of another phase of expansion, the development of our natural gas resources.
I said a moment ago that this is a billion dollar project, and so it is, but the Leader of the Opposition and his colleagues in this house are apparently unable to take in the entire picture. They apparently can see only a small corner of the canvas, that corner which is occupied by the short-term loan the government proposes to make to the private company which has undertaken to construct and operate the trans-Canada pipe line. The fact that many of the officers and principal shareholders of this company are Americans seems to offer irrefutable proof to the members of the Conservative party that the government of Canada is ready and willing to sell this country down the Mississippi.
May I ask why it is that these gentlemen from the United States are willing to take a multi-million dollar gamble here in Canada? Is it not because they have more faith in Canada than some Canadians themselves have? If there is a flow of United States risk capital into this country is it not because little or no Canadian risk capital can be found? It is an unfortunate fact that those who proclaim their love of Canada most loudly, and who are shrillest in their denunciation of foreign infiltration, economic, social or political, are least inclined to invest personally in any phase of Canada's development which has not already, through the courage and foresight of others, become established as a sure thing. They not only want to have

their cake and eat it too, they want someone else to do the baking and take the first bite to make sure it is palatable.
On the subject of the suspected "sell-out" we have heard here in the house repeated references to the Minister of Trade and Commerce as a dictator, a man who is prepared to sacrifice public interest to political expediency. I think the answer to that is simply that if the people of Canada held this same belief there would now be a different Minister of Trade and Commerce.
But the people of Canada do not believe this. They know that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is a doer, not a dictator. He is a bottleneck breaker, a production man turned to politics. If enterprise, to quote the Royal Bank letter of May 1956, is the doing of things, then the minister is a man of enterprise because he gets things done. Being a good production man he hates waste, either of money or of time. And at the present stage of the trans-Canada pipe-line project time is even more valuable than money.
We have reached a point in Canada's national progress where additional sources of energy are urgently required. Less than 10 per cent of our total energy is in the form of electricity. The remaining 90 per cent is found in fuel of one kind or another, coal, oil, wood or gas. Hence, natural gas is not in itself a competitor with electricity. Its development as a source of energy will take place within the 90 per cent non-electric area, and therefore its productive potential is almost unlimited.
The United States is now served by a tremendous network of natural gas pipe lines, pipe lines which provide about 25 per cent of all the energy consumed in that country. Moreover, it is predicted that in the near future natural gas consumption for domestic purposes will equal that of oil in the United States, and that within one year there will be no substantial section of the states which is not supplied with natural gas services. It is estimated that one out of every two houses in the United States is using natural gas at the present time. In comparison, gas provides only 6 per cent of the total energy consumed in Canada. Obviously there is a national need for making our western gas reserves available to the rest of the country.
The province of Ontario will require additional sources of energy, other than electricity, within the next six years. Ontario is looking for low-cost energy, and natural gas is the answer.
The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) stated this evening that Quebec is not interested in natural gas. I do not know 67509-268J

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation about the city of Quebec or the city of Three Rivers, but I do know about Montreal. In Montreal there is no shortage of hydroelectric power, and there will be no shortage for at least 25 years. However, Montreal is one of the most expensive cities in America when it comes to buying coal. Because of Ontario's relative proximity to the Ohio and Pennsylvania coal fields coal laid down in Toronto is much cheaper than the same coal laid down in Montreal.
Consequently when the trans-Canada pipe line reaches Montreal it will have a beneficial effect upon the fuel situation. Because of its competitive qualities natural gas will not only provide an efficient and cheaper source of heat but it will also bring about a reduction in the consumer cost of coal and oil. This will of course 'be to the direct advantage of domestic consumers, householders and apartment dwellers.
Further, it will materially help Montreal to maintain its position as Canada's metropolis, in spite of the rapid expansion of other cities. The high cost of fuel in Montreal has had the effect in the past of discouraging the establishment of certain industries there, inasmuch as fuel is a major cost factor in the production of goods. As a result, the coming of natural gas to Montreal will place that city in a better competitive position with respect to other manufacturing and industrial centres.
The domestic consumer will benefit in many ways from the availability of natural gas. Like other large cities, Montreal is bursting at its residential seams. Areas which once were small suburbs are now the scene of great housing developments. Former country villages are now city suburbs. What a few years ago was farmland is now urban property. This movement toward the periphery will continue for many years to come.
Once the trans-Canada pipe line has been laid into Montreal, feeder lines can be hooked on to it to supply new residential districts. Thus there will not be the initial construction expense of providing for large central heating units in houses, nor the operating expense of buying more expensive fuels to heat the houses. Even in the older, long-established residential areas, where no gas supply system exists and where it would be uneconomic to introduce such a system now, residents will find the coming of natural gas a benefit, since it will bring down the price of other fuels.
There is also an important national defence aspect, so far as the Montreal area is concerned. Oil supplies to Montreal come from sources outside Canada, principally the South American countries, and during wartime the

A rather more specialized but none the less important field is the production of petrochemicals. A very limited supply of these hydrocarbon by-products is now obtained from Montreal oil refineries, but there is a virtual ceiling on their production. Natural gas will raise that ceiling substantially, if not remove it altogether.
I should like to restate a point upon which I touched earlier. When I speak of energy resulting from natural gas, I am speaking of the fuel aspect rather than the power aspect, the supplying of heat rather than lighting or the turning of wheels. The province of Quebec, and particularly the industrial and manufacturing area of Montreal, must adopt the use of low-cost natural gas if it is to keep pace with industrial development in Ontario.
Canada's economic and social development in recent years has not been the result of occult forces working beyond our human understanding. It has been the result of careful planning and courageous action. The prime function of good government is to create the atmosphere in which progressive planning can be done and productive action can be taken. The present government has created and maintained such an atmosphere. It has not rushed heedlessly into disaster, but neither has it hung back in indecision when the moment arrived for positive accomplishment.

I should like to remind the house again of something which I think the government at least seems to have forgotten. This is not a mere single pipe line which is being constructed. This approach to the problem at this time is going to establish a basic definitive policy for the transportation of gas in Canada for all time to come. It is a historic breakthrough in that connection. It is not an isolated example. It is establishing a basic policy. Therefore when we consider this matter we have to look at it not in the light of a single isolated example, not in the light of particular geographical or local interests, but in the light of the future policy of Canada and the future development of this country.
Within that framework, Mr. Speaker, I think it is pretty generally agreed that if a country is to grow, prosper and develop, then control of its own economic interests must rest within its own borders. In that respect there is nothing wrong with the investment of foreign funds in a country. That is a good thing. But there is something radically wrong with foreign control of a country or foreign control of any major economic field in that country. That is bad. I suggest that as a touchstone in this whole matter, as a basic approach to it, we should be seeking something which will give us the maximum foreign investment needed in Canada with the minimum foreign control.
I suggest to you further, Mr. Speaker, that this particular bill is a complete reversal of that process. It gives us, as far as I can see, a minimum of foreign investment with a maximum of foreign control and is completely abhorrent to the other proposition I put forward, which I certainly think is in the best interests not only of the economy of Canada but of the economy of any country.
If we are going to encourage foreign investment in Canada it is certainly necessary that we know the fields in which this should be done, and I suggest that transportation is one field in which, while possibly welcoming investment, we should fight against control.
I think one can put forward in support of that argument something that one might call the vital industry theory. I suggest that there are the usual two breakdowns of any country's economy, the primary, which is the extraction of raw materials, and the secondary, which is their production into finished goods. Early in the morning, my friend has corrected me quite accurately, and this is the 65th address in the debate on this proposed legislation, I hope I will be able to add something to what has been said already.
In the course of this debate the position of the various parties has become transparently clear. The C.C.F. position from the first has been the support of public ownership of the line to transport gas across Canada. They brook no compromise with that position; it is outright public ownership. The position the Conservative party has now taken is that there should be a reference of this matter to a committee in order to determine whether the line can be financed by Canadian capital, and if it cannot then there should be public ownership. The position of the Liberal party, of course, is that this line should be constructed by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines.
In the course of this debate, when the house has been sitting long hours and when feelings have been strong on the issue, there have been many things said, attacks upon people, which I think will not commend themselves to the judgment of many of the electors. I do not propose to indulge in any way in that type of debate. I believe the facts in this case are so eloquent that if they are only stated to the people they will agree that the solution adopted by the Liberal government is the only possible solution under the circumstances. May I just remind hon. members that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines was incorporated in 1951, and Western Pipe Lines at about the same time. In 1953 when they applied to Premier Manning of Alberta for permission to export gas from Alberta, Mr. Manning said that neither, independently, was qualified, and he asked the Prime Minister if he would use his good offices to bring these two companies together.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce undertook that task and in January, 1954, he brought together the people who had backed Trans-Canada Pipe Lines and Western Pipe Lines Limited. The result was that this company, made up of new interests as well as
4230	HOUSE OF
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation the old but retaining the old name, made application to the premier of Alberta for permission to export gas from Alberta. I think, technically speaking, the application was made to the petroleum board of Alberta. In any event, permission was granted to Trans-Canada to export 500 million cubic feet daily from Alberta, of which 200 million cubic feet could be exported to the United States via Emerson and they were obliged to reserve 300 million cubic feet for Canadian use. I need not recall the debates that took place in this house when all parties were agreed that the trans-Canada pipe line should run through an all-Canadian route.
Following permission to export gas from Alberta, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines obtained permission from the board of transport commissioners to lay their pipe across Canada. They also proceeded to make arrangements with the suppliers of gas in Alberta, and they proceeded to arrange for the distribution of gas to the consumers. I believe that Trans-Canada does not deal with the consumers directly; it deals with distributing companies. The result was that in 1954 Trans-Canada was in a position where it could try to arrange its finances.
After investigation it found that it could not successfully finance the project under the set-up that existed at that time. It was not economically feasible; therefore an application was made to this government for help. The government refused to guarantee bonds, as was first requested, to be issued by the Trans-Canada company. The company then made application to the industrial development bank, but the terms laid down by the bank were such that they could not be accepted by the Trans-Canada company.
That brought the company up to 1955. In that year it made arrangements with Tennessee Gas Transmission Company to sell 200 million cubic feet daily in the Minneapolis market via Emerson. If it had been able to make those sales Trans-Canada was confident that it would be able to finance the line. As hon. members know, the right to transport and sell gas in the United States depends upon the permission of the federal power commission. The opponents of the backers of Trans-Canada opposed the application before the federal power commission. Northern Natural Gas Company had previously a contract with Trans-Canada and they spearheaded the attack before the federal power commission, as a result of which no decision has been given by the federal power commission.
It was under those circumstances that the Trans-Canada company approached the government, and the result is the proposal we
[Mr. Carrick.i

now have before the house. It proposes that Trans-Canada construct the line from the western end of Alberta to Montreal, Quebec, and that the western section be financed to the extent of 90 per cent of the cost, not to exceed $80 million, by the government. The western section is to extend from Alberta to Winnipeg. Trans-Canada is to construct the line from Winnipeg to the western boundary of Ontario.
Under the proposal the federal government, together with the Ontario government, is to construct the line from the western border of Ontario to Kapuskasing, Ontario, at a cost of $118 million, and Trans-Canada is to carry the line from Kapuskasing, Ontario, down to Toronto and to Montreal, Quebec. This is the proposal now before the house.
The position of the Conservative party is that Trans-Canada should not be assisted as long as there is a possibility of the project being financed from Canadian capital. Anyone who has perused the documents of Mr. McMahon tabled by the Minister of Trade and Commerce will see, as has been mentioned on a number of occasions in this house, that they involve a condition which makes it absolutely impossible for the government to accept the proposal. The necessary condition of that proposal was that 400 million cubic feet daily be exported to the United States via Minneapolis, which would leave only 100 million cubic feet daily available for the Canadian market, which is only one-third of the requirement of the Canadian market.
The only other proposal put forward was put forward by Gairdner and Company. Their proposal was inadequate because, among other things, they asked for a 10-year exemption from income tax. That was unacceptable to the government. Even in their last letter they said that they might be able to eliminate that on certain conditions, but they did not say what the conditions were. Besides, the government were not satisfied, in spite of what they said, that Gairdner and Company could get the pipe.
I do not think it has been mentioned in the house that Gairdner and Company contemplated constituting a corporation in which Trans-Canada was to have a part of the equity. One needs only to state that to hon. members to indicate how impossible it would be for Gairdner and Company to make any such arrangement. So the net result was that there was no Canadian company that could possibly finance this project. The fact has been mentioned often that the only company that has pipe available to start construction in 1956 is the Trans-Canada company.

Now, it must be obvious to everyone that in these circumstances there was only one company available to carry on this project. It may have come as a surprise to some hon. members to see the urgency that was established by the evidence in the letters of Mr. Manning, premier of Alberta, and of Mr. Campbell, premier of Manitoba, and of Mr. Porter, treasurer of Ontario. Anyone reading those letters could have no doubt whatsoever why it was absolutely necessary to get the western end of the pipe line constructed this year. That was the situation in which the government found itself.
I would like to submit for the consideration of the house some suggestions in connection with the charge that has been made that the Canadian taxpayers' money should not be used to finance Trans-Canada because at the present time it is about 83 per cent controlled in the United States. I think all hon. members will agree with me that all parties in this house are in favour of importing capital from the United States. The Leader of the Opposition has made it quite clear that when he was premier of Ontario he took steps to see that this was done, and all parties are agreed upon that. I think all parties will agree that if imported capital is to be brought in from the United States, that capital is entitled to a fair return on its money.
I point out this fact to hon. members. What the government is doing in helping Trans-Canada in connection with the northern Ontario sector and in connection with the western section is to enable Trans-Canada to construct this pipe line and arrange its financing. This is the important point. It has been established that Trans-Canada will need to raise $257 million in order to construct this line in Canada. Well, that $257 million can be raised only in two places. It can be raised either in Canada or in the United States. If it is raised in Canada everybody is in agreement that it is a good thing; and if it is raised in the United States everybody is in agreement that it is a good thing because it imports capital into Canada. Under these circumstances, how can there be any reasonable objection to the proposal that the government makes to help the Trans-Canada line?
I wish to deal for the moment with the charge that this is a sell-out of Canada's natural resources. The owners and the large suppliers of gas in Alberta include Canadian Gulf, which owns about one-third of the supply and is the largest owner. I am now refreshing hon. members' memories on certain facts given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Hudson Bay Oil and Gas is the second largest owner and Canadian Delhi is the fourth. At the present time these three

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation companies are backers of Trans-Canada to the extent of 58-9 per cent. In other words, the backers of Trans-Canada are merely trying to a large extent to sell their own gas. I ask hon. members in all fairness in these circumstances how it can be suggested that any group of persons who are trying to sell what they already own are selling out the natural resources of Canada?
A great deal has been made of the monopoly position of this company. I do not want to embark on a discussion of monopolies or the policy of this government as laid down under the Combines Investigation Act. I point out to hon. members, however, that under the Combines Investigation Act there is nothing wrong with being a monopoly. It is only when a monopoly operates or is likely to operate to the detriment of the public that there is anything objectionable to it. I think it would be a very difficult task to prove that the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines company, with its rate of profits which can be controlled by the federal government and with the price the distributors can charge to the consumers controlled, would be acting in a way that is detrimental to the Canadian public.
Mr. Speaker, time alone will prove whether or not the legislation before the house is in the interest of Canada. I am confident that time will vindicate the judgment of this government and that the trans-Canada pipeline project will stand as a monument to the courage, foresight and wisdom of this government and the great Liberal party of Canada.

But it was interesting to note that in old Bruce county, where so many people have been Liberals for so many years this girl by the name of Mackenzie who had never heard about the C.C.F. was disturbed at the prospect presently before Canada.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier was one of my heroes when I was a lad, and he felt that closure was most unbecoming in this Canada of ours. He said:
But, sir, I also have the honour to belong to the great Liberal party of Canada. I have occupied

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation a position of some importance in it; nay, I may say that for twenty years and more I have been entrusted with its chief command. During the fifteen years I was in office it sometimes happened that friends came to me and told me that I was not doing justice to myself and to the party, but that I should impose closure, as had been done in many other parliaments. Sir, I am a Liberal of the old school; I have been brought up in the school of Fox and of the old leaders of the Liberal party; and I could not bring myself to the point of depriving a minority in parliament of such a valuable weapon as it would be deprived of by the introduction of closure.
And then later:
Let me repeat to my right honourable friend: As you sow, so shall you reap; as you are fair, so shall you meet with fairness; as you are unjust, so shall you meet with injustice. . . . The poison that he offers to us today will come to his own lips at some future day. We are in the minority; we can be gagged; we can be prevented from expressing our opinions; they can trample upon our rights; sir, the day of reckoning will come, and it will come as soon as we have a dissolution of the present parliament.
I submit that the performance we have witnessed here is unbecoming to any democratic country. The government has been unwilling to allow us to discuss this question at sufficient length, as is indicated by the interruptions I have had during the major part of my time tonight. I was simply trying to reply to remarks which were in order when the Minister of Agriculture was on his feet, when the hon. member for Rosthern was on his feet, and when the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre was saying everything that was so pleasing to the government.
The proposal to build this pipe line under public ownership really would not place any strain on the resources of Canada, and no one knows this better than the Minister of Trade and Commerce. This is the minister who developed T.C.A. at a time when private enterprise was not prepared to put risk capital into such an uncertain venture. I remember when the Minister of Trade and Commerce got $50 million from the public treasury for Polymer. The large rubber and petroleum companies might have been expected to put in risk capital, but when we lost our source of natural rubber the Minister of Trade and Commerce risked his reputation and risked $50 million of the money of the Canadian people to try out this new process for the manufacture of rubber. I think the experience we have had in those two fields should demonstrate that this important development should be undertaken from the beginning under public ownership.
I know the problems of management that we have had in Saskatchewan. The Minister of Trade and Commerce knows that he has trained a great many young people in his department who have been picked up by private enterprise and paid double the salaries

he was able to pay. That is a matter of real concern to every cabinet minister in this house. That is the retaining in the public
service of some of our best people when such large salaries are being offered by private enterprise, when the corporations which pay these high salaries can dip into the public treasury by means of the corporation tax to compel the taxpayers to pay salaries which are sometimes three or four times as high as these men would have had in the public service.
So I suggest that the government should face up to the fact that it cannot ask the people of Canada to bail out a corporation of which 83 per cent is controlled south of the border when they are unwilling to risk more than a very small percentage, and when they refuse to move unless they are guaranteed that they will have the taxpayers of Canada run the real risks.

Mr. Speaker, this is a rather historic occasion. It is 24 years since closure was last used in this house. I would point out that the history of closure has shown that it has not been a profitable course to follow. People generally look on it as a way of stopping free speech and as a way of circumventing parliament and the people; consequently they view it with a certain amount of alarm.
Changing the subject, I want to say something about the pipe line. There are a few questions that could be asked the government by the people as to just what is going on. One of the questions they are almost certain to ask is why the unseemly haste, when five years have elapsed since the granting of the charter to this company and their time has been extended from time to time. If there was all the urgency that the government would now like to convince parliament and the people exists, why did they not do it the first time the company defaulted some three years ago, and not wait until four months after parliament had convened to urge upon us that there was some emergency?
There is an answer behind this activity, too. Governments, whether they be paternal, autocratic, totalitarian or democratic, are not eternal. Therefore, in this government's lifetime, this line must be built for its friends. That is the motive behind this unseemly haste during the past few days. The question arises, who are the people that are actually behind this Trans-Canada Pipe Line company? They are primarily-not entirely, but primarily,-those Americans who now own and control the gas resources in Alberta.
Then there is another question that should be asked. What about Canadian markets? There is a very strange silence at that particular level. Apparently there is a wait and see attitude in the municipalities, towns and cities. There is one answer, however, that is obvious; and that answer is that the consumer will not buy unless it is sold at a competitive price. I would say from my talks with residents in Ontario that I cannot find any pronounced demand and enthusiasm or any crying need for immediate gas supplies. As a long-range proposition, I would say yes without hesitation; but even then there is a question mark in my mind. Will the atomic age make the gas pipe line obsolete just as the atomic age and the age of the airplane made the Maginot line in Europe obsolete?
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation
Then another question arises. The company having assured the parliamentary committee that there was abundant financing available without any difficulty, that there were abundant supplies of gas and there was an eastern market and, above all, that there would be a Canadian line, what do we find? We find that until the federal power commission in the United States grants permission for the importation of Canadian gas into the United States the Trans-Canada company is not interested in proceeding. We find also that the original intention of the company, though well disguised, was not to supply eastern Canada but to supply a lucrative market south of the border.
So, after five years of jockeying for position, where do we find ourselves? Trans-Canada Pipe Lines have so manipulated the course of events that the Canadian people are being forced by the government under closure and threat of further closure to finance in large measure a privately-owned pipe-line venture largely for the direct benefit of a small number of United States interests holding vast supplies of Canadian gas.
Then there is another question. Will eastern Ontario and Quebec consumers benefit? I would say not appreciably, because the gas will be sold at the highest competitive price at which it can be sold. Then there are other considerations. As far as I can find out, no cities and towns have evinced publicly any great desire to secure western gas, and it is quite within the realm of possibility and, in fact, I would say it is more than likely that Canadians will be asked to subsidize this line further after it has been completed so that the price of gas in the east can be made competitive with the prices of other fuels. I think this matter should be very seriously considered. I can see deficits and further votes of public funds might well be the order of the day for parliaments of the future, maybe for years to come.
As far as the western leg of the line from Alberta to Winnipeg is concerned, I can understand and appreciate the interest and desire of those provinces to have the line completed at the earliest possible moment. I can see where it is a great asset to those western provinces, but once again I ask: Why should the province of British Columbia, all of the province of Quebec beyond the city of Montreal and the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland have any enthusiasm for such a project?

Then there are some other angles that should also be considered. Probably not many Canadians are aware of the fact that during the second great war thousands and thousands of users of gas were deprived of fuel because the Americans refused supplies to the southwestern Ontario region, particularly the city of London. During the war thousands of people had to remove the gas equipment from their furnaces and reconvert to some other fuel.
When the chips are down, Mr. Speaker, the Americans do not hesitate to look after their own interests first. Whether it be a gas line, whether it be tariffs or trade relations, the United States of America comes first on every occasion. The question arises whether we are prepared to subsidize private interests. I rather think we should not. But I believe Canadians are prepared to subsidize, if necessary, Canadian ownership, however distasteful it may be, rather than see the line owned and controlled by United States interests. It is my opinion that it is better to guarantee bonds sold to Canadians than to guarantee profits to Americans.
There is another question I want to bring to the attention of the house. I cannot support the C.C.F. amendment because it precludes all the other angles that we have sought to bring before a committee. I believe the line can be built by private industry and without the use of the taxpayers' money. Then there is another point. No member is entitled to vote upon any question in which he has a direct pecuniary interest, and a vote of any member so interested will be disallowed.
Under the provisions of that standing order, Mr. Speaker, I rise to challenge the vote just cast for the second reading of Bill No. 298 by the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Nickle). May I say that I am sure the hon. member for Calgary South will agree with me that this is the type of matter that we should approach very seriously; for he himself said

on January 15, 1953, when he was criticizing the former Liberal member for Westmorland, as recorded at page 1053 of Hansard for that [DOT]day:
A member of parliament should be, like Caesar's wife, above suspicion.
I wish to make it perfectly clear that, as I understand the rules of the house, there is no question whatsoever as to the legal right of the hon. member for Calgary South, despite what I shall say in a moment, to apeak as he has done on this legislation. For my part, I had nothing to do with any efforts to prevent him from speaking. It was his right to speak and he exercised that right. But, Mr. Speaker, the same rules make it quite clear that if one has a direct pecuniary interest in a measure he should not vote thereon, and if he does vote his vote should be disallowed.
The information on which I raise this point is found in documents which are matters of record. I refer to the Parliamentary Guide, and I also refer to the Financial Post's directory of boards of directors. One can ascertain from these documents that the hon. member for Calgary South is the president, the vice president or a director of at least nine oil, gas or pipe-line companies. I do not intend to take the time of the house, nor do I intend to confuse the issue, by reading the names of all the companies of which my hon. friend is president, a vice president, or a director, but I single out one in particular, namely Bailey-Selburn Oil and Gas Limited, of which my hon. friend is a director.
I find in the Financial Post survey of oils, 1956, that Bailey-Selburn Oil and Gas Limited has signed a contract with Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited to supply gas from the Buffalo-Bindloss field to the pipe line when operations commence. That fact, namely that this company of which my hon. friend is a director has a contract with Trans-Canada Pipe Lines to supply gas to that company when operations commence, is also indicated in the Financial Post for Saturday, December 24, 1955. My decision had been based upon several reasons which I have voiced many times in this house. I believe in sound economic planning. However, when it became apparent that I would have to take a stand in support of this particular company in order to get a pipe line built at all-and costs are certainly rising which rule out any further delay-and to avoid the building of a pipe line with a far higher cost to the taxpayers of this country, I then had to make another decision.

The next step taken concerns my relationship with the companies with which I have chosen to continue as a director during my term in this house. I emphasize again that the directorships of the several independent Canadian oil companies with which I was associated prior to becoming a member of this house are with companies in which I believe, and I shall do my best to support them as companies in which I think Canadians

I have resented very strongly some of the statements made by the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Nickle), when he has imputed to my colleagues the suggestion of political expediency; but I defend his right to express his opinion, and I would hope that the right to express independent opinions will be recognized on both sides of this house.
The question of direct pecuniary interest is not an easy one to resolve. I need not mention the cases which have arisen in regard to certain hon. members wherein this problem has been raised. In this case I am not in any way referring to the question of the relationship of directorates or matters of that kind, but this problem in this complex system of ours is not an easy one. Many people may have holdings in certain companies without any possible suggestion of impropriety. I think it would be most unwise and most unfair if on a motion of this kind and on a bald declaration that an hon. member has

certain shareholdings and certain associations, the right to vote, which after all is the right of membership in this house, should be dealt with by an arbitrary decision which permits of no examination of the facts.
There are procedures available. If any hon. member feels that any other hon. member is contravening the rights of membership in this house, we have a committee on privileges and elections before which such a subject can be properly raised. Under those circumstances the hon. member himself whose position is challenged would then be able to state the facts fully and answer any imputation that might be made as to a conflict of his own personal interests. The responsibility for that course is one that can be assumed by any hon. member. The course which is now proposed is one under which the members of this house would be asked to pass judgment upon another hon. member without an appropriate opportunity to examine the facts and to give that hon. member a chance to meet specifically the allegations that are made.
This is a difficult subject, one which has raised great difficulties, in this parliament, at Westminster and elsewhere in places which operate under a parliamentary system similar to ours. Certainly in this complex society of ours the personal interests of the hon. members of this house should not be dealt with in any arbitrary manner. They should certainly not be dealt with in a way which would deny full opportunity to meet any allegations stated in the most specific form.
For the reasons I have stated I hope the hon. members of this house will see fit to vote against the motion which has been made.

subtopic: FREIGHT ASSISTANCE, WESTERN GRAIN
FREIGHT ASSISTANCE, WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
1.	When was the freight assistance policy on western grains introduced?
2.	What is the total amount paid in connection with this policy on movements to Nova Scotia, since the start of the assistance?
Answer by: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
1. The freight assistance policy on western feed grains was introduced in October 1941.
2. The amount paid on the movement of western feed grains into Nova Scotia up to April 30, 1956, was $20,657,188.75.

MARITIME MARSHLAND REHABILITATION ACT
speechtext:
1.	How much has the federal government paid to date for works undertaken in Nova Scotia under the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act?
2.	How much has been spent in this connection in the constituency of Cumberland?
Answer by: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
1.	As at March 31, 1956, $3,559,764.46.
2.	As at March 31, 1956, $1,006,282.01.
